questions.q: Sarah's team is building a hostel booking app. Which of these decisions should they stop on, writing alternatives and getting a review?
questions.hint: Which ones involve stored data or an outside system?

options.text: Which type to use for storing booking money in the database
options.why: That's the data model. Once hundreds of thousands of bookings exist, changing the type means moving every row, and a wrong type muddles the money totals too.

options.text: The shape of the API response given to partner hostels
options.why: A public contract. Partners will write code against it, so you won't be able to change it alone later.

options.text: Which folder the test files live in
options.why: A folder can be moved in an hour any day, and nobody outside notices.

options.text: Which Vue component handles date picking
options.why: It's confined to one or two files; if it's wrong, you can swap it in a day or two.

questions.q: What is the long-term problem in the code below?
questions.hint: Exactly which fields does the client receive, and who decides that list?

options.text: `$this->json()` is slow; `new JsonResponse()` should be used
options.why: The two do almost the same job. Speed isn't the problem here.

options.text: The User table's structure becomes the public contract — changing a column will break clients
options.why: The entity's properties are the JSON fields. So every internal change reaches the outside, and even secret fields can leak.

options.text: It should be POST rather than GET
options.why: GET is the right method for reading data.

options.text: There's no problem — the less code, the better
options.why: Less code today, but the moment you change a column tomorrow you'll have to coordinate with every client.

questions.q: "Which database to use" is cheap to change on day one and very expensive two years later. What is the main reason?
questions.hint: What has been built on top of the decision in two years?

options.text: The database software gets old
options.why: Version upgrades are a separate, comparatively easy job. That isn't where the cost comes from.

options.text: The license price goes up over two years
options.why: Prices may rise, but the effort of changing comes from somewhere else.

options.text: Two years of stored data, and hundreds of queries written in that database's dialect
options.why: The more stands on a decision and the more data piles up, the costlier a change gets.

options.text: Developers don't want to learn another database
options.why: Learning takes a few weeks; moving data and queries takes months.

questions.q: A team lead says, "Every decision is important, so we'll hold a meeting on each." What is the real harm?
questions.hint: Time is limited. If every decision gets an equal share, how much do the expensive ones get?

options.text: The expensive decisions get no special attention, and the whole team slows down
options.why: If button colors and the data model get equal time, it's the data model that loses out, though mistakes there cost the most.

options.text: No harm — more discussion always means better decisions
options.why: A long discussion of a cheap decision saves nothing, because a mistake can be fixed in an hour anyway.

options.text: More meetings make the code quality worse
options.why: The number of meetings isn't the problem; the problem is spending the time in the wrong place.

questions.q: Which of these quietly turn a cheap decision into an expensive one?
questions.hint: Where are many things leaning directly on something internal?

options.text: Two separate apps reading and writing the same table directly
options.why: The table's structure becomes the contract between the two apps — even renaming one column forces both teams to deploy together.

options.text: Using a vendor's SDK classes directly in 40 files
options.why: Switching vendor means touching 40 places. Behind an interface it would be one class.

options.text: Splitting one private method into three smaller ones
options.why: Nobody outside sees a private method; it's tidying inside a class and can be changed any time.

options.text: Using the database's auto-increment id in public URLs
options.why: The internal id becomes an outside promise; changing the id type breaks every old link and client.

questions.q: Which of these is usually NOT an architectural decision?
questions.hint: Which one can be changed by touching just one class?

options.text: Whether orders and payments live in one service or two
options.why: That's a service boundary, one of the four foundations. If it's wrong, code, data and teams must be re-split.

options.text: Whether money is a float or integer cents
options.why: That's the data model. It's hard to change once data has piled up, and a wrong type gives wrong totals too.

options.text: Which email-sending library sits behind an interface
options.why: The rest of the code knows only the interface. Switching libraries means rewriting one class — a paint-like decision.

options.text: The field names in the API given to the mobile app
options.why: A public contract. You can't force an old app on a phone to change.

questions.q: Which of these are one-way door decisions, where you should stop and think?
questions.hint: Which ones can't be reversed if wrong, or cost a lot to reverse?

options.text: Dropping a column from the production database
options.why: Deleted data doesn't come back without a backup, and rolling back the code doesn't bring the column back.

options.text: Removing a field from a public API
options.why: External clients wrote code against that field. Removing it breaks their apps, and that's out of your hands.

options.text: Putting the new checkout behind a feature flag
options.why: Turning the flag off brings the old path back, so this is a two-way door.

options.text: Adding a new nullable column
options.why: Old code doesn't know the new column, so nothing breaks, and you can drop it later.

questions.q: The migration below and the code change went out in the same deploy. A bug showed up in the code and you rolled back to the previous version. What happens?
questions.hint: A rollback restores the code. Does the database state come back with it?

options.text: The old code asks for the `phone` column again, but it's gone, so errors follow
options.why: Even when the code is rolled back, the migration doesn't undo itself. And even if it did, the column's data wouldn't come back.

options.text: Everything works, because the rollback restores the database too
options.why: A deploy rollback restores only the code. Database changes have to be reversed separately.

options.text: Only new users will have problems
options.why: Anyone whose request makes the old code read `phone` hits the problem, new or old.

questions.q: Ryan's team wants to switch SMS companies, but the SDK's classes are spread across 30 files. What is the best step for the future?
questions.hint: How do you bring the places to change down from 30 to 1?

options.text: Put the SDK behind an `SmsGateway` interface and have all the code call that
options.why: Then switching company means rewriting just one adapter class.

options.text: Add the new company's SDK next to it in all 30 files
options.why: That doubles the dependency and locks the door even tighter.

options.text: Drop the idea of switching, since going back is hard
options.why: If it's hard, there's a way to make it easy, and an interface is that way.

options.text: Run a find-and-replace across all the files
options.why: It's risky and you'd have to repeat it every time; the real problem, the spread-out dependency, remains.

questions.q: The new checkout ran behind a flag for an hour and charged 40 customers twice by mistake. You switch the flag off. What is still true?
questions.hint: What does a flag control: code, or the world outside the code?

options.text: New orders use the old path again, but the 40 double charges still exist and must be refunded
options.why: A flag chooses the code path. Money already taken is outside the flag and needs its own fix.

options.text: Everything is back as before, including the 40 charges
options.why: The charges are real records at the payment provider. Switching code does not cancel them.

options.text: The flag cannot be switched off once customers have paid
options.why: The flag can always be flipped. It just does not clean up the past.

questions.q: You copied `phone` into `mobile_number` and switched the code to read it. Before dropping `phone`, which result of this query tells you it is safe?
questions.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customer
WHERE phone IS NOT NULL AND mobile_number IS NULL;
questions.hint: What would a non-zero count mean?

options.text: 0: no number exists only in the old column
options.why: Every old value is already in the new column. With a backup, the drop will not lose data.

options.text: Any number above 0, because rows exist in both columns
options.why: The query counts rows that have phone but lack mobile_number. A positive count means data would be lost.

options.text: The query result does not matter if the tests pass
options.why: Tests rarely cover every old row in production. The query checks the real data.

questions.q: What is the best rule for deciding how much time to give a decision?
questions.hint: Think about the consequence of a mistake, not the size of the decision.

options.text: Decide reversible things fast, and irreversible ones slowly and in writing
options.why: Where a mistake is cheap, speed wins; where it's permanent, verification wins.

options.text: Give every decision equal time so nothing is missed
options.why: Then the expensive decisions don't get enough time, and the cheap ones slow the team down.

options.text: Spend more time on whichever decision looks bigger
options.why: A small-looking migration can be one-way, and a big-looking job can be a two-way door behind a flag.

options.text: Decide everything fast; you can fix it later
options.why: For decisions you can't fix, this rule destroys data or trust permanently.

questions.q: Which is the correct expand-contract order?
questions.hint: The new thing comes first; deleting the old comes last.

options.text: Add the new column, copy the data, make the code read the new one, then drop the old column
options.why: The old column stays intact in every step, so you can safely go back until the last one.

options.text: Drop the old column, then add the new one and copy the data
options.why: If the old data is deleted before copying, there's nothing left to copy.

options.text: Start reading the new column in the code, then add the column
options.why: Reading a column that doesn't exist yet is an error right away.

options.text: Everything together in one migration
options.why: Doing it all at once leaves no chance of going back midway, and that is the trap.

questions.q: Ryan's team wants to take a shortcut under deadline pressure. Which of these make it "good debt"?
questions.hint: What is known and what is settled in good debt?

options.text: Writing the shortcut in the debt register, with its interest
options.why: Written down, the debt stays in everyone's sight, and knowing the interest shows why repaying matters.

options.text: Settling who repays it and by when
options.why: Without an owner and a date, "we'll fix it later" never arrives.

options.text: Leaving a small comment in the code without telling anyone
options.why: If nobody knows and there's no ticket, nobody will ever look for that comment.

options.text: Assuming the rules can't be followed and taking shortcuts in the rest too
options.why: One shortcut invites another. That sends the debt out of control.

questions.q: A new developer says, "We never knew about layering, so we put queries in every controller." Which kind of tech debt is this?
questions.hint: Was the debt known beforehand?

options.text: Inadvertent and reckless: nobody knew the debt existed
options.why: Debt built from lack of knowledge, which nobody wrote down. This is the most dangerous box.

options.text: Deliberate and prudent: a tactic to save time
options.why: Deliberate would mean taken knowingly, but here they didn't even know the alternative.

options.text: It isn't tech debt, just personal preference
options.why: Preference or not, the result is the same: every future change gets slower.

options.text: Deliberate and reckless
options.why: Deliberate and reckless means knowing the better way and avoiding it; here nobody knew the better way.

questions.q: What important piece of debt management is missing from the comment below?
questions.hint: Who will look for it later, where is it recorded, and when must it be done?

options.text: A ticket number, an owner and a repayment date, so someone can track it
options.why: Without a ticket nobody finds a TODO, without an owner nobody does it, and without a date it always waits for later.

options.text: A PHPDoc type annotation
options.why: Types improve code quality, but they have nothing to do with tracking debt.

options.text: A longer comment written in more detail
options.why: Length doesn't make something tracked; you need a ticket and a date.

options.text: Nothing, writing TODO is enough
options.why: Numberless TODOs pile up and turn into lost debt.

questions.q: You have two debts. A: code touched every week, 2 days to repay. B: code nobody touches, 1 day to repay. Which first?
questions.hint: Where is the interest piling up faster?

options.text: A, because interest piles up faster where it's touched every time
options.why: Interest is paid whenever you touch the code. The higher the interest, the bigger the gain from repaying.

options.text: B, because it takes less time to repay
options.why: The order depends on interest, not on how quick the fix is. Nobody touches B, so it has no interest.

options.text: Both together, because all debts are equal
options.why: Debts aren't equal. Without ordering by interest, your time goes to the wrong place.

options.text: Neither, new features come first
options.why: Neglect A and every new feature will be slower.

questions.q: You will merge `BlackFridayCheckoutService` into `CheckoutService`. What do you do first?
questions.hint: How will you know the merge changed nothing by accident?

options.text: Write a test that sends one fixed cart through both classes and records the totals
options.why: It pins today's behavior, so after the merge a red test shows exactly what changed.

options.text: Delete `BlackFridayCheckoutService` and fix whatever breaks
options.why: You would be debugging live orders instead of a test, and rules hidden in the copy could be lost.

options.text: Add a third class that wraps both
options.why: That adds a layer without removing the duplication, so the interest keeps growing.

options.text: Add a TODO comment and merge next year
options.why: A TODO without a ticket, owner and date never gets done.

questions.q: The team lead says, "Let's pause features for two months and rewrite the whole system." What is the biggest risk of this approach?
questions.hint: Where do the small rules hidden in the old system go?

options.text: The old code's hidden rules get dropped, and it doesn't finish in two months
options.why: Old code carries years of bug fixes and rules. A rewrite loses many of them, and it takes longer than estimated.

options.text: The new code will be slower than the old
options.why: Speed isn't the main problem here; the risk is losing rules and not finishing.

options.text: The team won't learn anything new
options.why: They'd actually learn. The risk is elsewhere.

options.text: There's no risk, because new code is always clean
options.why: New code also piles up debt quickly under pressure, especially around rules nobody knew about.

questions.q: Which of these are real costs of microservices?
questions.hint: Think about the difference between a method call inside one process and a network call.

options.text: Calls between services are slow and can fail
options.why: On a network you need timeouts, retries and handling of partial failure, none of which a method call needed.

options.text: One feature's data is split across several databases, so transactions break
options.why: An ACID transaction in one database doesn't cross service boundaries, so reconciling data becomes a separate job.

options.text: The code always has to be rewritten from PHP into another language
options.why: Changing language isn't mandatory. That's an option, not a cost.

options.text: Each service needs its own deploy, log and monitoring
options.why: The more services, the more deploy pipelines and the more places to look.

questions.q: What problem does the code below create?
questions.hint: What inside Billing is the Shipping module holding on to?

options.text: Shipping is tied to Billing's entity, so the boundary exists only in the folder name
options.why: If Invoice's table changes, Shipping breaks, and later splitting Billing into a service becomes hard.

options.text: It should be OneToMany instead of ManyToOne
options.why: The direction of the relation isn't the problem; the problem is a relation crossing a module boundary.

options.text: Doctrine annotations are outdated, so this is wrong
options.why: This is an attribute, which is correct in modern Doctrine.

options.text: No problem, they're in the same app anyway
options.why: Even in one app, ignoring boundaries ends the modular monolith, and everything gets tangled.

questions.q: Shipping needs to know whether an order is paid. Which design keeps the modular monolith intact?
questions.hint: Which design uses only the public door of Billing?

options.text: Shipping injects Billing's `InvoiceRepository` and reads the status
options.why: It reaches past the public door into Billing's internals, so a change inside Billing breaks Shipping.

options.text: Shipping adds a `ManyToOne` to Billing's `Invoice`
options.why: The relation ties Shipping to Billing's table, so the boundary exists only in the folder name.

options.text: Shipping stores only the order ID and calls `BillingApi::isPaid($orderId)`
options.why: Only Billing's public door is used, so Billing can change inside, or become a service later, without Shipping noticing.

options.text: Copy Billing's invoice table into Shipping's schema and keep both in sync by hand
options.why: Two copies of one fact drift apart, and now two modules own the same data.

questions.q: A team of eight is starting a new booking app. What is the smartest way to begin?
questions.hint: The team is small, the boundaries are still unknown and features change fast.

options.text: A modular monolith with modules by business capability and clear boundaries
options.why: You get a simple deploy, and wrong boundaries are easy to fix. Later, if there's a reason, you can split a module off.

options.text: Every feature a separate service from the start
options.why: The boundaries aren't known yet, and a wrong cut is hard to correct inside services.

options.text: One app with no boundaries, code however you like
options.why: That makes the biggest complaint about monoliths, the tangle, come true.

options.text: A separate database, and everything else in one file
options.why: Splitting data alone doesn't make a boundary; boundaries are needed in both code and data.

questions.q: A company built "UserService", "DatabaseService" and "NotificationService", all using the same database. Adding one feature touches all three. Where is the problem?
questions.hint: What are the boundaries based on, and who owns the data?

options.text: The boundaries follow technology, and the data has no single owner
options.why: Boundaries by business capability would keep a feature in one place, and everyone writing to one database makes a distributed monolith.

options.text: There are too few services
options.why: The number isn't the problem; what the boundaries are based on is.

options.text: Writing services in PHP is wrong
options.why: The language is irrelevant here.

options.text: The network is slow
options.why: A slow network would slow everything, but a feature touching three places comes from wrong boundaries.

questions.q: Which of these is a reasonable reason to turn a module into a separate service?
questions.hint: Look for organization and scale needs, not "popularity".

options.text: It needs a very different scale from the rest of the app, and a separate team owns it
options.why: A separate team and separate scaling make the cost of running a service worthwhile.

options.text: Big companies do it this way
options.why: Their teams and problems aren't like yours; their solution can be a burden for you.

options.text: The code feels a bit messy
options.why: Splitting messy code into services makes it more complex; fix the modules and boundaries first.

options.text: To learn a new technology
options.why: For learning there are small projects; in production everyone bears the cost.

questions.q: Which layering rule does the code below break?
questions.hint: What does the business rule know that it shouldn't?

options.text: The service knows HTTP's `Request`, so the dependency runs from bottom to top
options.why: The rule can't be used without HTTP. The controller should pull out the value and call the service with a plain `float` or a DTO.

options.text: A 90% discount shouldn't be given
options.why: Whether the calculation is right is a separate matter; the layering mistake is holding a `Request`.

options.text: A readonly class can't have __invoke
options.why: A readonly class can have __invoke without any trouble.

options.text: There's nothing wrong with this code
options.why: The rule is tangled up with HTTP, so it can't be used from a console command or a queue handler.

questions.q: The developers decide to freeze the old app and rewrite everything in six months. What problems does this have compared with the strangler fig?
questions.hint: Does the old app stand still for six months?

options.text: The old app keeps changing during the rewrite, so the new one is always behind
options.why: It's hard to keep two codebases in step, and even when the new one is finished it lags behind the old.

options.text: The old code's hidden rules can get lost
options.why: Years of bug fixes live in the code, not in documents. A rewrite drops them.

options.text: Users get the new system step by step
options.why: That is a strangler fig benefit. In a full rewrite everyone gets the new system at once, so mistakes are found late.

options.text: A router has to be installed
options.why: Installing a router is a strangler fig step, not a full-rewrite one.

questions.q: A legacy API returns the balance as the string "1250.50". Where in the new code should it be converted to integer cents?
questions.hint: Where do you confine the old system's language?

options.text: In a translator (ACL) class, so the new code only ever sees `balanceCents`
options.why: The translation lives in one place, and if the old format changes, only that changes.

options.text: In every controller that needs the balance
options.why: If translation is scattered, the old system's language leaks into new code and changes have to be made everywhere.

options.text: When formatting in a Twig template
options.why: A template is for display, not for data conversion.

options.text: No need to convert; you can calculate with the string
options.why: Money handled as strings or floats goes wrong; integer cents is safe.

questions.q: Which of these are a controller's job?
questions.hint: Think of the waiter's job: take, call, hand back.

options.text: Binding and validating the request into a DTO
options.why: Handling the language of HTTP is the controller's job.

options.text: Calling a service and choosing the response status
options.why: Calling the work and shaping the HTTP reply is the controller's responsibility.

options.text: Calculating the discount on orders above $100
options.why: Business rules belong in a service or the domain.

options.text: Writing straight to a table with SQL
options.why: Storing data is the repository's job.

questions.q: The checkout now gives first orders 15% off, but the admin page still shows the old price. What is the real fix?
questions.hint: How many places should know the discount rule?

options.text: Copy the new rule into the admin page as well
options.why: It fixes today, but you now have three copies that will drift apart again.

options.text: Move the rule into one class, such as `DiscountPolicy`, that the checkout, the other API and the admin page all call
options.why: One change updates every caller, and the rule gets a single test.

options.text: Add a comment above each copy: "keep in sync with checkout"
options.why: Comments don't run. The next change will still miss one copy.

options.text: Hide the price on the admin page
options.why: That hides the symptom. The two places still disagree.

questions.q: In a strangler fig setup, what config change in the router moves one path from the old app to the new one?
questions.hint: How does changing one rule in the router make the switch?

options.text: Pointing that path's `location` rule at the new app
options.why: One line moves the path, and removing that line moves it back.

options.text: Deleting the old app's code
options.why: Deleting is the last step; first you shift the traffic and check the results.

options.text: Changing the database
options.why: Changing the database is a separate, big decision; moving a path doesn't need it.

options.text: Giving users a new URL
options.why: Users stay on the same URL; the router switches the path behind the scenes.

questions.q: The new app and the old app share an `orders` table. The new app wants an integer `total_cents` instead of `total`. What is the safe order of steps?
questions.hint: Which step can't be undone, and when is it safe to take?

options.text: Rename `total` to `total_cents` in one migration
options.why: The old app still selects `total` and breaks at once.

options.text: Give the new app its own copy of the database and never sync them
options.why: Two databases mean two versions of every order, so orders placed on one are missing on the other.

options.text: Add `total_cents`, backfill it, move the new app over, and drop `total` only after the old app is gone
options.why: Each step is safe for the old app, and the one step that can't be undone comes last.

options.text: Drop `total` first, then add `total_cents`
options.why: The old app breaks, and the data in `total` is lost before it was copied.

questions.q: Which of these cause problems if kept on a server's local disk when you run several servers?
questions.hint: Can another server see this thing?

options.text: Profile photos uploaded by users
options.why: A request that lands on another server won't find the photo. Keep it in object storage.

options.text: PHP session files
options.why: On another server the session isn't recognized, and the user is logged out.

options.text: A temporary zip file created and deleted within a single request
options.why: The file lives and dies inside one request, so no other server ever needs to see it.

options.text: The deployed code, which is the same on every server
options.why: The code is deployed identically everywhere; it is not state.

questions.q: What is wrong with the config below if the app runs on two servers?
questions.hint: Where are session files written, and can the other server read them?

options.text: Session files sit on each server's own disk, so the other server doesn't recognize them
options.why: The `var/sessions` folder is local to the server. Fix it by keeping sessions in Redis or the database.

options.text: Setting handler_id to null stops sessions from working at all
options.why: File-based sessions work fine. The problem is that they aren't shared between servers.

options.text: %kernel.project_dir% is invalid syntax
options.why: The syntax is fine. The problem is conceptual.

options.text: Nothing, because the files are safe
options.why: They are safe on one server, but behind a load balancer you will get the logout problem.

questions.q: Alex's app builds a 10-minute report once a night at 2 a.m. and does nothing the rest of the day. Which option fits best?
questions.hint: Most of the time there is no work, and the work is short.

options.text: Serverless or a scale-to-zero container, so you pay only while the job runs
options.why: For irregular, short-lived work, pay-per-use is cheap.

options.text: A big server running all day just for this job
options.why: It sits idle for more than 23 hours a day and still costs money.

options.text: Building the report inside a user's request
options.why: Holding a request open for 10 minutes will time out. This belongs in a queue or a scheduled job.

options.text: Dropping the report
options.why: Dropping work the business needs isn't a solution.

questions.q: A Lambda-based Symfony app suddenly gets 1,000 users at once. What problem is most likely?
questions.hint: What do many instances do to the database all at the same time?

options.text: Many instances start together and exceed the database's connection limit
options.why: Each instance opens its own connection. Without a connection pool or proxy, the database gets overwhelmed.

options.text: All requests get stuck on a single instance
options.why: A serverless platform does the opposite: it creates more instances.

options.text: The code turns from PHP into another language
options.why: The language never changes.

options.text: Nothing, because serverless means unlimited capacity
options.why: The database, outside APIs and the platform itself all have limits.

questions.q: Which is the strongest argument for making the app stateless instead of using sticky sessions?
questions.hint: What happens when a server dies or is replaced in a deploy?

options.text: Users don't lose their sessions when a server dies or is replaced
options.why: When state lives outside, any server can read it, so work carries on even if one server dies.

options.text: Sticky sessions cost more because they don't use Redis
options.why: Cost isn't the point; sticky sessions are less reliable.

options.text: A stateless app needs less code
options.why: The aim is less fragility, not less code.

options.text: A stateless app doesn't need a database
options.why: The database matters more, because that is where the state goes.

questions.q: Nicole adds Flysystem, but her config points `uploads.storage` at a folder under `var/` in production. What happens with two servers?
questions.hint: Which disk does each server write to?

options.text: Each server keeps its own files, so a photo uploaded via Server A is a 404 on Server B
options.why: A local adapter writes to that server's disk. Production needs the S3 adapter so every server shares one bucket.

options.text: Flysystem copies the file to every server automatically
options.why: Flysystem only talks to the adapter you configure. It does not replicate between servers.

options.text: Nothing, because the code only stores a key in the database
options.why: The key is only a name. The bytes still live on one disk, and the other server cannot find them.

questions.q: Which of these are good, measurable requirements?
questions.hint: Does it have a scenario, a measure and a number?

options.text: "With 500 people arriving at once in a flash sale, the product page p95 is under 400ms"
options.why: It has a scenario, a measure and a target, and a load test can verify it.

options.text: "Monthly uptime >= 99.9%"
options.why: It has a measure and a number. It means no more than about 43 minutes of downtime a month.

options.text: "The system will be very secure"
options.why: There is no way to measure it, nor any value that would count as "very".

options.text: "The site should never be slow"
options.why: "Never" and "slow" are both vague; it doesn't say how slow, or in what situation.

questions.q: What is missing from this requirement?
questions.code:
- id: QA-3
  attribute: performance
  scenario: 'When a user searches'
  target: 'fast response'
questions.hint: How fast? What will be measured?

options.text: A measure (such as p95 latency) and a numeric target (such as < 200ms)
options.why: "Fast response" can't be measured. Without a number, nobody can say whether the work is done.

options.text: A longer scenario description
options.why: A longer description doesn't help without a measure.

options.text: A different id format
options.why: The id isn't the problem here.

options.text: Nothing, it's fine as it is
options.why: "Fast" means five different things to five people, so there is no way to verify it.

questions.q: A client says, "We need 99.999% uptime." What's the best response?
questions.hint: Get the client to think in terms of business loss.

options.text: Ask "What does an hour of downtime cost you?" and match the target to that loss and the price
options.why: Each extra nine costs many times more. If the cost exceeds the loss, it's wasted money.

options.text: Say "OK" and move on
options.why: Cost and complexity will multiply, and the client doesn't know that.

options.text: Say "That's impossible" and end the conversation
options.why: It isn't impossible, just very expensive. It needs a discussion.

options.text: Quietly decide on 99% yourself
options.why: Choosing a number without knowing the client's losses is just a guess.

questions.q: Downtime costs a shop $1,200 an hour. Moving from 99.9% to 99.99% saves about how much a month?
questions.hint: $1,200 an hour is about $20 a minute. How many minutes of downtime does the extra nine remove?

options.text: About $780: roughly 39 fewer minutes of downtime
options.why: 99.9% allows about 43 minutes and 99.99% about 4, so 39 minutes at about $20 each is around $780.

options.text: About $1,200
options.why: That is the cost of a whole hour. The extra nine removes only about 39 minutes of downtime.

options.text: About $46,800
options.why: That treats the saved time as hours. It is minutes: 43 minutes down to 4.

options.text: About $80
options.why: That is what the remaining 4 minutes of downtime still cost. The saving is the 39 minutes that disappear.

questions.q: Ian added a cache and made the product page 10 times faster. What price might he pay in other qualities?
questions.hint: What does a cache store, and when does stored data get old?

options.text: A risk of stale data, plus the cost and complexity of running the cache
options.why: A cache serves stored answers, so it may show an old price after a change. Invalidating it correctly is extra complexity.

options.text: Security improves
options.why: A cache doesn't improve security; a misconfigured one can even show one user's data to another.

options.text: There is no price, only benefit
options.why: Every quality has a price. For a cache it is stale data and complexity.

options.text: Availability drops because a cache shuts the whole server down
options.why: A cache usually helps availability or leaves it unchanged. The cost is elsewhere.

questions.q: How should quality priorities differ between a personal blog and a mobile banking app?
questions.hint: Which one does more damage when it breaks?

options.text: Banking puts security and availability first; the blog puts cost and maintainability first
options.why: The damage is different. A banking failure costs money and trust, while a blog can survive a few hours down.

options.text: Both should max out every quality
options.why: Paying for top availability on a blog is a waste.

options.text: The blog puts security first, banking puts cost first
options.why: That's backwards. A money app can't cut corners on security to save money.

options.text: There is no need to set priorities
options.why: If you don't, the argument comes after the release, when changes are most expensive.

questions.q: An app has 2 million DAU, and each person makes 10 requests a day. The busy-hour factor is 5. Roughly what is the peak QPS?
questions.hint: First requests per day, then divide by 100,000, then apply the factor.

options.text: About 1,000 QPS
options.why: 2 million x 10 = 20 million a day. Divided by 100,000 that is 200 average QPS. Times 5 is 1,000 at peak.

options.text: About 200 QPS
options.why: That is the average QPS. You forgot the peak factor.

options.text: About 200,000 QPS
options.why: You forgot to divide the daily requests by the seconds in a day.

options.text: About 10 QPS
options.why: That is 100 times too small; you canceled too many zeros when dividing.

questions.q: What is the mistake in this calculation?
questions.code:
200,000 parcels x 8 events x 200 bytes = 320 MB/day
1 year = 120 GB
Decision: a 200 GB disk is enough, with a year to spare.
questions.hint: Is raw data all that goes on the disk?

options.text: It ignores indexes and replicas, so the real space needed is much larger
options.why: Indexes and replicas take 2-3x the raw data. 120 GB could become 240-360 GB.

options.text: The bytes-to-MB conversion is wrong
options.why: 320 MB is right: 200,000 x 8 x 200 = 320 million bytes.

options.text: A year is not 365 days
options.why: 320 MB x 365 is about 120 GB, which is correct.

options.text: There is no mistake
options.why: The real mistake is counting only the raw data.

questions.q: Ryan says, "5 million requests a day is enormous load, we need 10 servers." What's right about that?
questions.hint: What is 5 million divided by 100,000?

options.text: It's about 60 QPS on average and 300 at peak, so a few servers are enough and 10 is wasteful
options.why: Spread across the day the number is small. Without the sum, you waste money.

options.text: He is right, 10 are needed
options.why: The sum gives 300 QPS / 150 = 2, plus 1 spare.

options.text: No calculation is possible
options.why: A rounded calculation is possible, and easy.

options.text: A single server is enough
options.why: At a 300 QPS peak one server isn't enough, and if it dies the site goes down.

questions.q: Which of these are true?
questions.hint: By how much does each step slow things down?

options.text: Reading from RAM is far faster than reading from SSD
options.why: RAM is nanoseconds, SSD is microseconds. That is why caches live in RAM.

options.text: A network call inside the same data center is practically free
options.why: It takes about 0.5 ms, which becomes a large cost when you chain many calls.

options.text: 1 million requests a day is about 12 QPS
options.why: 1 million / 86,400 is about 12.

options.text: A round trip between continents takes about 1 ms
options.why: The speed of light limit makes it about 150 ms.

questions.q: What is the best way to present the result of an estimate?
questions.hint: Should an estimate look exact?

options.text: "2 to 5 servers, assuming a 5x peak and 150 QPS per server"
options.why: The range and the assumptions are both out in the open, so anyone can check or change them.

options.text: "We need exactly 3.42 servers"
options.why: Making an estimate look exact is false precision.

options.text: "We'll need a lot of servers"
options.why: Too vague to act on.

options.text: "It can't be calculated, so let's skip it"
options.why: A rough sum is possible and enough; skip it and you won't catch a 10x error.

questions.q: The QPS sum gives 3 app servers. The database and Redis each need one machine too, at $200 a month per machine. What is the monthly bill?
questions.hint: Count every machine, not only the app servers.

options.text: About $600
options.why: That is 3 machines x $200. It leaves out the database and Redis.

options.text: About $1,000
options.why: 3 app + 1 database + 1 Redis = 5 machines, and 5 x $200 = $1,000.

options.text: About $400
options.why: That counts only the 2 machines needed for capacity and drops both the spare and the other services.

questions.q: A team of four has 2,000 users and needs to do some work, like sending email, in the background. Someone says, "Let's install Kafka, we'll need to scale later." What is the best decision?
questions.hint: First check whether what you already have can do the job.

options.text: Use Symfony Messenger with the PostgreSQL or Redis you already run as the queue
options.why: There is no new technology to run, yet the job gets done. If you really need more later, you can change Messenger's transport.

options.text: Install Kafka, because changing later will be hard
options.why: This load needs no Kafka, but you'd carry its running burden from day one. With Messenger, changing transport later isn't hard anyway.

options.text: Write your own queue system
options.why: Everyone needs a queue in the same way, and tested solutions are close at hand. Building it wastes time, and the bugs would be yours.

options.text: Send the email inside the request, since any queue is complexity
options.why: Adding Messenger on an existing database costs almost no complexity, and it really does solve the problem of making users wait.

questions.q: If you run an open source search engine on your own server, which of these costs will you pay?
questions.hint: Think of the free recipe: what is free, and what is on you?

options.text: The monthly server bill
options.why: The software may be free, but the machine to run it isn't.

options.text: The time to apply version upgrades and security patches
options.why: When you run it, keeping it updated is your job; skip it and you leave security holes.

options.text: The software license fee
options.why: This is usually the one cost that is zero in open source, and people look only at it and think everything is free.

options.text: Your own team's time to fix it when it breaks at midnight
options.why: With SaaS that's the vendor's job. When you run it yourself, the phone call comes to your team.

questions.q: For building reports there are two roads: SaaS at $2,000 a month, or build it yourself for 60 engineer-days, then 3 days of maintenance a month. One engineer-day costs $500. Which is right on a three-year view?
questions.hint: Build = initial days x $500 + monthly days x $500 x 36. SaaS = monthly bill x 36.

options.text: SaaS is cheaper: $72,000 vs $84,000 for building
Building is cheaper: $30,000 vs SaaS at $72,000
options.why: $30,000 is only the initial cost. It leaves out $54,000 of 36-month maintenance, the most familiar TCO mistake.

options.text: Building is cheaper because there is no monthly bill
options.why: There is no bill, but there is engineer time, and that is the largest cost.

options.text: They are equal, so pick the more modern one
options.why: The numbers aren't equal. And even if they were, risk and team skills would decide, not novelty.

questions.q: What is the long-term problem in the code below?
questions.hint: If AcmePdf triples its price tomorrow, how many files must change?

options.text: Vendor classes sit directly in business code, so switching vendors means rewriting every such place
options.why: With no interface in between, the vendor's name and way of calling it spread through the code. That is lock-in.

options.text: Two vendors are used together when one would have been enough
options.why: Using different vendors for different jobs is normal. The problem isn't the number but how tangled they are with your code.

options.text: Buying PDF and email services was the mistake; they should have been built in-house
options.why: Both are things everyone needs in the same way, so buying is the right call. The mistake was not leaving an exit door.

options.text: The class being final prevents switching vendors
options.why: `final` only blocks inheritance. What blocks switching is the vendor's class sitting right inside.

questions.q: For an online bookshop, which of these are reasonable to build yourself?
questions.hint: Which jobs set this shop apart from other shops?

options.text: Your own rules for recommending books from a reader's history
options.why: This could be the shop's edge; a ready-made solution doesn't know this business's special knowledge.

options.text: Your own password-hashing algorithm
options.why: Building security primitives yourself is dangerous. Symfony's password hasher has been tested for years.

options.text: Your own payment gateway for taking cards
options.why: It involves licenses, compliance and huge risk, and customers see no added benefit. Buy it.

options.text: Your own rules for an offer that swaps old books for new ones
options.why: This rule is specific to this business, no ready-made tool will have it, and it is what attracts customers.

questions.q: A new project is starting. Everyone on the team knows PostgreSQL well. An ad for a new database says "twice as fast". What should you do?
questions.hint: Is speed a measured problem right now, or just something in an ad?

options.text: Start with PostgreSQL, and consider alternatives only if a measured problem appears
options.why: A familiar technology means fewer surprises and quicker fixes. Spending complexity budget on a problem you don't yet have makes no sense.

options.text: Take the new database, because faster means better
options.why: There is no guarantee the ad's speed applies to your workload, and the team doesn't know how the unfamiliar technology fails.

options.text: Use both at once, to cover every angle
options.why: Two databases means double the running cost and the extra work of keeping data in sync, with no gain.

options.text: Delay the decision and benchmark both for six months
options.why: Six months of benchmarks for a problem you don't have is waste too. Starting with the familiar tool is fastest and safest.

questions.q: Nicole's video site freezes whenever someone uploads a video, because the conversion runs inside the web request. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: Where does the heavy work belong in a video pipeline?

options.text: Rewrite the web app in a language that benchmarks faster
options.why: The web language was not the bottleneck. The conversion would still block the request, just in a different language.

options.text: Save the upload to object storage, and convert it in a background worker
options.why: The request returns at once, and a worker handles the slow conversion. The web app stays responsive whatever language it uses.

options.text: Buy a bigger server so conversion finishes sooner
options.why: It only postpones the problem. Ten uploads at the same time still tie up ten web requests.

options.text: Ask creators to upload smaller videos
options.why: This hides the design flaw behind a user rule, and it hurts the product.

questions.q: Which of these are questions about the job to settle before shortlisting a framework?
questions.hint: Pick the questions about the job, the team and support, not about popularity.

options.text: How strict are the correctness needs, such as money and audit?
options.why: It decides how much you value ready-made, proven protection.

options.text: Which stack got the most stars on GitHub this month?
options.why: Popularity says nothing about your workload or your team, and it changes every month.

options.text: What can the team run and operate, and who can we hire?
options.why: A stack nobody can maintain is a risk, however good it is.

options.text: What does the framework already provide built in?
options.why: Every built-in is code you do not write, test or patch.

options.text: Which stack did the last conference speaker use?
options.why: That is fashion. The speaker's job is not your job.

questions.q: A claims system must apply discounts to the exact cent and keep every change traceable. What should weigh most in choosing the stack?
questions.hint: Think about the fragile cargo question.

options.text: Raw requests per second in a benchmark
options.why: Speed matters little if the totals are wrong. Correctness comes first in this job.

options.text: Exact decimal handling, strict transactions and an audit trail, preferably ready-made and proven
options.why: These are the needs that cost real money when they fail, and a mature stack gives them to you tested.

options.text: How good the stack is at serving video
options.why: It is a different job with a different workload shape.

options.text: How new and exciting the syntax is
options.why: Novelty adds learning cost and unknown failure modes, which this job can't afford.

questions.q: Which parts of a video site are usually handled outside the web framework?
questions.hint: Follow the file from upload to the viewer's phone.

options.text: Converting videos into several sizes in a background worker
options.why: It is slow work, so it runs in a worker with a converter such as ffmpeg, not inside a request.

options.text: Delivering popular videos from a CDN
options.why: A CDN keeps copies close to viewers, so the app server is not carrying the video traffic.

options.text: Storing the original and converted files in object storage
options.why: Big files go to a store built for them, not to the application database.

options.text: Deciding whether a logged-in user may edit a channel
options.why: This permission check is business logic. It lives in the web backend.

questions.q: A team of five knows Django well and must build accounting software for a small firm. What is a sensible decision?
questions.hint: No stack is wrong. What must you check?

options.text: Switch to Java, because accounting needs Java
options.why: No stack is required. Switching spends complexity budget and loses the skills the team already has.

options.text: Use Django, but store money as floats since the team knows them
options.why: Floats cannot hold some decimal values exactly. Money needs exact decimal types whatever the stack.

options.text: Use Django with exact decimal fields and database transactions, and add a tested audit-log library
options.why: It uses the team's skill and adds what the job needs. The checks are the right ones: decimals, transactions, audit.

options.text: Delay the project until every framework has been benchmarked
options.why: A benchmark doesn't answer the correctness and audit questions, and the delay costs more than it saves.

questions.q: Which is a real price of choosing a framework that ships many built-in features?
questions.hint: There are two sides to the trade-off. Which side is this?

options.text: More to learn and more ceremony, even for small jobs
options.why: A bigger framework has more concepts, and a small job pays for them too.

options.text: You must write your own transaction handling
options.why: The reverse: built-ins mean you do not write it.

options.text: It can no longer integrate with other systems
options.why: Frameworks do not stop integration. They often make it easier.

options.text: Its releases are never supported for long
options.why: Mature frameworks often offer long-term-support releases, which is part of why enterprises pick them.

questions.q: Kevin's month-end report is slow, and someone proposes rewriting the system in a benchmark-winning stack. What should happen first?
questions.hint: What would you do before spending a year?

options.text: Start the rewrite and migrate module by module
options.why: It spends a lot of effort on a guess, and the real cause may be a single query.

options.text: Adopt the benchmark winner for new modules only
options.why: This mixes two stacks and spends complexity budget without evidence of a need.

options.text: Measure where the time goes and fix that part, for example with an index
options.why: It is cheap, quick and reversible, and it keeps the stack where the rules and people already live.

options.text: Add a second database so reports can run on both
options.why: A second database doubles the running cost, and you still have not found the cause.

questions.q: A company with three layer teams (UI, Backend, DB) takes 3 weeks for every feature. What is the best step?
questions.hint: Is the delay in writing code, or in the handoffs?

options.text: Form full-stack teams around business capabilities (such as Catalog and Checkout)
options.why: A feature finishes inside one team, so handoffs and waiting shrink.

options.text: Hire two more people into each team
options.why: More people don't shorten the queue; the delay is in handoffs and waiting, not in the amount of work.

options.text: Write a more detailed ticket template
options.why: Better tickets reduce misunderstandings, but they don't cut the wait in three queues.

options.text: Move all the code into a single repository
options.why: Even in one repository the teams' ownership split remains, so the handoffs stay the same.

questions.q: Which of these are part of the inverse Conway maneuver?
questions.hint: Remember the order: system divisions first, then the teams.

options.text: Drawing the boundaries of the modules you want first
options.why: This is step one. Without the architecture you want, there is nothing to arrange the teams against.

options.text: Deciding on one owning team for each boundary
options.why: A boundary without an owner doesn't last. The owning team's natural communication is what protects it.

options.text: Keeping existing teams as they are and building the system in their mould
options.why: That is just letting Conway's Law do what it likes, not using it on purpose.

options.text: Writing a contract (interface or API) between teams
options.why: A boundary isn't only a line; it is also the rules for crossing it.

questions.q: A company splits into two big teams, but the code stays as it was and everyone works in the same folder. What will you see after a few months?
questions.hint: If the boundary isn't in the code, what will hold the team split?

options.text: The two teams will step on each other's code, with more merge conflicts and surprise breakage
options.why: With no boundary in the code, the team split exists only on paper. The friction stays as it was.

options.text: The code will split in two by itself
options.why: Code doesn't split by itself. You have to do it deliberately, with boundaries and ownership.

options.text: All the problems will go away because the teams are smaller
options.why: Even with smaller teams, if they share the same code their work will collide.

options.text: Nothing will change, because organization and code are unrelated
options.why: Conway's Law says they are related. A mismatch increases friction.

questions.q: What is wrong with the Checkout team's code below, from a boundary point of view?
questions.hint: What happens if the Catalog team renames a column?

options.text: Checkout depends directly on Catalog's entity, so a change in Catalog will break Checkout
options.why: The internal entity is the Catalog team's private business. Depending on it without a contract means there is no boundary.

options.text: findOneBy is slow and find should be used
options.why: Speed isn't the issue here. The issue is whose code has reached into whose internals.

options.text: The class is final, so it can't be tested
options.why: `final` doesn't prevent testing. The broken boundary is the real problem.

options.text: Nothing, because both modules are in the same database
options.why: Even with one database, the code is owned separately; sharing it only raises the risk of breakage.

questions.q: In which situation can teams and services be called well matched?
questions.hint: Look at both ownership and capacity.

options.text: Every service has one owning team, and the team can handle it
options.why: Responsibility is clear and the boundary fits the team's capacity. You need both.

options.text: All three teams can commit to every service, so nobody gets blocked
options.why: When everyone owns it, no one is responsible, and the code gets messy fast.

options.text: There are twice as many services as teams
options.why: The count isn't the measure. Ownership and team capacity are.

options.text: One team looks after every service, so everything is in one place
options.why: If the team is large and the load heavy, no service runs well, and then splitting into services means little.

questions.q: For three months, every feature a team shipped changed the cart, price and order services together, and never one alone. What should they do?
questions.hint: Services that always change together are really what?

options.text: Add more retries and timeouts between the three services
options.why: That makes the calls more reliable, but the three still need a change and a deploy every time.

options.text: Treat them as one boundary: merge them into one module with one owner
options.why: The history shows they were split in the wrong place. One module means one pull request and one deploy per feature.

options.text: Give each service to a different team to speed things up
options.why: Every feature would now cross three teams and three queues, the problem from the first slide.

options.text: Nothing, because separate services are always better
options.why: Separate services pay off only when they can change independently. These cannot.

questions.q: The team rule: no Doctrine in Domain code. What is the most reliable way to enforce it?
questions.hint: People get tired and forget. CI doesn't.

options.text: Add Deptrac or PHPat rules and run them in CI, so a violation turns the build red
options.why: It is measured automatically on every pull request, and nobody can forget.

options.text: Write the rule on the wiki in bold
options.why: Even when it is written down, if it isn't measured nobody knows whether the code is drifting.

options.text: Have a senior engineer read the whole codebase every month
options.why: Slow, expensive, and human eyes skip small imports anyway.

options.text: Tell new team members the rule in person
options.why: Spoken rules get forgotten, and even longtime members take shortcuts.

questions.q: Which of these are good fitness functions?
questions.hint: If it can report pass or fail automatically, it qualifies.

options.text: At most 10 queries on the list API, enforced in PHPUnit
options.why: A stable measure that runs on every PR and catches N+1 immediately.

options.text: A dependency rule: Domain knows no layer, enforced in Deptrac
options.why: Dependency rules can be measured automatically, so this is a good fitness function.

options.text: "We will keep the code clean": a team pledge
options.why: Sincere, but it can't be measured. So it is not a fitness function.

options.text: p95 under 300ms, with a k6 threshold in the nightly pipeline
options.why: Speed is measured, and the pipeline fails when the budget is exceeded.

questions.q: What is wrong with this deptrac rule set?
questions.hint: Look at the direction of the arrows: who knows whom?

options.text: Domain may know Infrastructure: the dependency points from inside to outside instead of outside to inside
options.why: It opens the door for Doctrine or HTTP code to enter the Domain. The rule should be `Domain: ~`.

options.text: Application knows only Domain, which is too little
options.why: Application knowing Domain is exactly right. The problem is on another line.

options.text: Infrastructure should not know both inner layers
options.why: Infrastructure knowing the inner layers is the correct direction.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, you can write anything in the ruleset
options.why: The ruleset is the architecture rule. Write it wrong and you guard the wrong thing.

questions.q: Your Deptrac config has layers Domain, Application and Infrastructure only. A developer adds `use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping` to a Domain class. What happens?
questions.hint: Where does Doctrine's code live, and what did the config name?

options.text: Nothing: Doctrine is not in src/ and is not a named layer, so Deptrac does not see it
options.why: Deptrac only judges layers you define. Add a Doctrine layer and give Domain an empty rule, and the same import fails the build.

options.text: The build fails, because Domain: ~ forbids every import
options.why: `Domain: ~` forbids dependencies on other layers. A library that is not a layer is invisible to the rule.

options.text: Deptrac fails because the class has attributes
options.why: Deptrac reads dependencies between classes, not attributes as such. It needs a layer to judge them against.

questions.q: The product list used to run 8 queries and now runs 54. What is the best way to catch this in CI?
questions.hint: Measure what is stable.

options.text: Put a limit on the profiler's query count in a functional test
options.why: With an N+1 the query count jumps at once and the test fails; the number is stable, so it isn't flaky.

options.text: Fail the test if it takes more than 200ms on the clock
options.why: CI machine speed varies, so the test would fail now and then for no reason.

options.text: Wait until users complain in production
options.why: By then users have gotten used to the slowness, and the cause is harder to find.

options.text: Put a cache on every query
options.why: A cache hides the problem rather than fixing it, and adds complexity of its own.

questions.q: A new project must send emails in the background. Someone says, "Let's install RabbitMQ now, or we'll be in trouble later." Which is the better decision by the last responsible moment?
questions.hint: How cheap is it to change the transport in Messenger?

options.text: Start with the Messenger doctrine transport; write down a trigger on message rate or lag and switch when it is hit
options.why: The decision is cheap (a DSN change), there will be more information later, and the trigger makes sure "later" really arrives.

options.text: Install RabbitMQ right now, because changing later will be hard
options.why: With Messenger it isn't hard to change; installing it now only adds operational burden.

options.text: Skip the queue and send the email inside the request
options.why: The user waits, and fixing it later means changing scattered code.

options.text: Say "we'll look later" without fixing any number
options.why: Without a trigger "later" never comes; it comes after the fire starts.

questions.q: The design says: "When the user presses Pay, the Payment API is called." Which question is the most useful in review?
questions.hint: What do people do when the network is slow?

options.text: If Pay is pressed twice or the request is retried, what reaches the Payment API?
options.why: This is the "what if it arrives twice?" question, and it is where the need for an Idempotency-Key comes from.

options.text: What color should the button be?
options.why: That can be changed in one afternoon; it doesn't deserve the review's precious time.

options.text: Which PHP version will this run on?
options.why: Useful to know, but it isn't a question that uncovers failure paths.

options.text: Who wrote this design, and are they experienced?
options.why: Judge the design, not the author. Experienced people have gaps too.

questions.q: Which problems in the code below should a design review catch?
questions.hint: What if the SMS is slow, fails, or the request runs again?

options.text: There is no timeout, so a slow SMS server will hang the request
options.why: With no wait limit, a dependency's slowness becomes our own slowness directly.

options.text: If the SMS fails the order is never confirmed, yet the SMS is not a condition of the main job
options.why: If `toArray()` throws, we never reach markConfirmed. The SMS should go through a queue.

options.text: If the request runs again the customer gets two SMS messages, and there is no key
options.why: A retry or a double click can send the same SMS twice; nothing provides idempotency.

options.text: flush() is called at the end and should have been called earlier
options.why: Ordering is a fair question, but the position of flush() isn't the main gap in this code.

questions.q: Everyone on the team likes the design and nobody objects, but the project feels risky. What should you do?
questions.hint: No objections doesn't mean it is safe.

options.text: Run a pre-mortem: assume the project has failed and have everyone write the reasons alone
options.why: Treating failure as having happened gives even quiet members the nerve to write down the risks.

options.text: Call an even bigger review meeting and walk everyone through the design again
options.why: You'd get the same happy-path discussion again, with no safe way to raise the risks.

options.text: Treat no objections as approval and move ahead
options.why: Silence is often pressure or optimism, not proof that the design is flawless.

options.text: Treat the most senior person's opinion as final
options.why: That just swaps the problem: one person's view is final and there is still no list of risks.

questions.q: Which of these are good design review comments?
questions.hint: A question, a risk, a suggestion, and never aimed at the person.

options.text: "If the payment times out, how will we know whether the money was taken? We could add a status check or a webhook."
options.why: It has a specific question, a risk and a suggestion, all three.

options.text: "This design is bad, rewrite it."
options.why: There is no reason and no path forward. The author gets defensive instead of learning.

options.text: "If sending the email fails, the order fails too. What about moving it to a queue?"
options.why: The risk is clear, and the fix is offered as a question.

options.text: "You're new here; why didn't you think of this?"
options.why: This attacks the person, not the design, and it shuts the discussion down.

questions.q: A design has the step: "save the order, then notify the inventory service". If the inventory service is 10 seconds slow, what is the biggest risk?
questions.hint: With no wait limit, where do the waiting threads pile up?

options.text: Waiting requests pile up and our own server becomes slow or unresponsive too
options.why: A slow dependency holds our workers or threads, so the slowness spreads. A short timeout and a queue are the remedy.

options.text: The inventory service will speed up on its own
options.why: Slowness doesn't fix itself; our own design needs a way to cope with it.

options.text: The order data won't be saved to the database
options.why: The save already happened; the problem is the wait after it.

options.text: No risk, 10 seconds is a small amount of time
options.why: At 50 requests a second, 10 seconds leaves about 500 requests waiting, each holding a worker. That is how a small slowdown becomes an outage.

questions.q: Your call to the payment API times out after 5 seconds. What should the order be?
questions.hint: Did we hear "no", or did we just stop listening?

options.text: Pending: we don't know the outcome, so ask again with the same Idempotency-Key or check the status
options.why: A timeout only means we stopped waiting. The same key makes the second ask safe: no second charge.

options.text: Failed, so the customer can pay again straight away
options.why: The money may already have been taken; a second payment would charge the customer twice.

options.text: Paid, because most calls that time out still succeed
options.why: It is a guess. If the charge did not happen, we would ship goods for free.

options.text: Retry in a loop without a key until it answers
options.why: Without a key every retry is a new charge, and a loop of retries is how a retry storm starts.

questions.q: From a hexagonal point of view, what is wrong with this use case?
questions.hint: What does the use case depend on: interfaces or real equipment classes?

options.text: The rules depend directly on Doctrine and Twilio; with no ports, tests are slow and switching vendors is hard
options.why: The real equipment has come into the use case's constructor. With interfaces (ports), these would live in adapters.

options.text: The class is `final`, so it can't be extended
options.why: final is not the problem here. The problem is the direction of dependencies.

options.text: `__invoke` should not be used; the method should be called handle()
options.why: A method name is a matter of taste; the architectural problem is elsewhere.

options.text: confirm() should live outside Order, not inside it
options.why: The rule belongs inside Order; moving it out would only tangle things further.

questions.q: Which of these classes should live on the outside (in Infrastructure) as "adapters"?
questions.hint: Which ones talk to outside equipment?

options.text: DoctrineOrderRepository
options.why: It talks to Doctrine and fulfills the port's contract, so it is an adapter.

options.text: SmsCustomerNotifier
options.why: It sends SMS through Symfony Notifier; everything about the vendor stays locked in here.

options.text: The confirm() rule of Order
options.why: That is a business rule, part of the inside. It has nothing to do with equipment.

options.text: The CustomerNotifier interface
options.why: That is a port, not an adapter. It is written from the inside, and the outside fulfills it.

questions.q: To cut costs you have to switch SMS vendors. In a hexagonal design, what is the right thing to do?
questions.hint: Which class knows the vendor's name?

options.text: Write an adapter for the new vendor (or change the Notifier DSN); the use cases and rules stay unchanged
options.why: The change is small precisely because knowledge of the vendor is locked inside one adapter.

options.text: Hunt through every use case and replace the vendor's SDK
options.why: That happens when hexagonal is missing, not because of it. Here the SDK lives only in the adapter.

options.text: Rename the port interface after the new vendor
options.why: A port speaks business language, not a vendor's name; renaming it would mean changes everywhere.

options.text: Install the new vendor's SDK in the Domain and update the rules
options.why: Putting a vendor in the Domain turns the dependency direction upside down.

questions.q: What is the best way to make ConfirmOrderHandler's test fast?
questions.hint: With a port in place, what can stand in for a real database?

options.text: Run the use case with an in-memory fake of OrderRepository and a spy Notifier
options.why: No network or database is needed, so the test finishes in milliseconds. Only the rule gets checked.

options.text: Mock Doctrine and script the behavior of every EntityManager call
options.why: It makes brittle tests tied to the internal design; with a port you don't need this contortion at all.

options.text: Use the real database and the real Twilio in the test
options.why: Slow, brittle, and it can cost money.

options.text: Skip testing the rules and only check in a real browser
options.why: Slow and unreliable; testing the rule directly is far faster.

questions.q: Which port design is fine?
questions.hint: Does the port's name use the language of the business or of the equipment?

options.text: `awaitingPaymentSince(DateTimeImmutable $time): array`
options.why: Written in business language; the adapter decides how the query runs.

options.text: `queryBuilder(): QueryBuilder`
options.why: Doctrine's type leaks out. The use case will build queries itself and the inside gets tangled with the database again.

options.text: `findByTwilioStatus(string $s): array`
options.why: A vendor's name has crept into the port. Switch vendors and the port itself is dead.

options.text: `executeSql(string $sql): array`
options.why: SQL has leaked out; this isn't a port, it is a door straight into the database.

questions.q: The business says "the customer canceled the order", and the code says `$order->setStatus(3)`. From a ubiquitous-language point of view, which change is best?
questions.hint: The business sentence should show up in the code almost word for word.

options.text: `$order->cancelByCustomer()`
options.why: The business's words made it into the code. Business people can read it, and "canceled by us" can be a separate method.

options.text: `$order->setStatus(OrderStatus::CANCELLED)`
options.why: Better than a number, but it still doesn't separate who canceled, and the rules are still easy to break from outside.

options.text: `$order->setStatus(3); // 3 = canceled`
options.why: A comment doesn't fix the language, and it doesn't say which cancellation the 3 means.

options.text: `$order->flag3 = true;`
options.why: A meaningless name moves you even further from the business language.

questions.q: The business says: "customer cancels, store credit; we cancel, refund." Which design makes the wrong-refund mistake hardest to repeat?
questions.hint: Which version lets a reader see the rule from the method name alone?

options.text: One `cancel(bool $byCustomer)` method
options.why: Better than numbers, but `cancel(true)` at the call site still says nothing, and both rules end up tangled in one method.

options.text: `cancelByCustomer()` and `cancelByUs()` as two methods, each followed by its own step (credit or refund)
options.why: Each business sentence is a method name, so a refund after `cancelByCustomer()` looks wrong at a glance.

options.text: One `cancel(int $type)` where 1 means customer and 2 means us
options.why: Numbers again: every caller must remember what 1 and 2 mean, which was the original problem.

options.text: Keep `setStatus(3)` and describe the numbers on a wiki page
options.why: The wiki and the code drift apart, and nobody opens the wiki at the moment they write the line.

questions.q: In an e-commerce system both the Sales and Support teams use the word "Customer", but their needs differ. What is the best decision?
questions.hint: What happens when one class keeps changing for two teams' needs?

options.text: Keep a separate Customer class in each context, linked by id
options.why: Each context models only what its own job needs, so one team's change doesn't break the other.

options.text: Put both teams' fields in one giant Customer class
options.why: The class becomes huge and confusing, and the two teams' changes break each other.

options.text: Force one team to use the other team's words
options.why: The meanings differ because the needs differ. Forcing it would hamper one team's work.

options.text: Drop the word Customer and run on numbers
options.why: Taking the language away makes the misunderstanding worse.

questions.q: Which of these are usually value objects?
questions.hint: Is "are they equal?" decided by an id or by the value?

options.text: Money ($500, USD)
options.why: Equal values mean the same thing; no identity of its own is needed.

options.text: Email (user@example.com)
options.why: The same address is the same email. Kept in a class, an invalid format can't even be created.

options.text: Customer (with an id)
options.why: It stays the same Customer even if the name and address change. It has an identity, so it is an entity.

options.text: Order (with an id)
options.why: The order stays the same even if its items change. It has an identity (id), so it is an entity.

questions.q: A developer writes `$cents = (int) ($price * 100);` with `$price = 19.99`. What is true?
questions.hint: What does (int) do to the decimals of a float: round or cut?

options.text: It is always 1999, because PHP rounds when casting a float to int
options.why: PHP truncates when casting a float to an int; it does not round.

options.text: It can give 1998, because 19.99 * 100 is 1998.9999999999998 and (int) cuts off the decimals
options.why: The float is not exact, so the product lands just under 1999 and the cast drops the rest.

options.text: It only goes wrong for amounts above a million dollars
options.why: Size does not matter. The tiny representation gap shows up at small amounts too.

options.text: Keeping the price as integer cents (1999) from the start avoids the conversion altogether
options.why: With whole cents there is no float and no multiplication, so nothing can be lost.

questions.q: Where does the aggregate's rule get broken in the code below?
questions.hint: Who is checking the item limit or the confirmed-order rule?

options.text: The controller changes the inner collection directly, so none of Order's rules (limit, status) are checked
options.why: It skips the root's `addLine()` and goes straight inside, so nobody is protecting the invariant.

options.text: Using status 201 is wrong
options.why: 201 is correct for creating a new resource; the architectural problem isn't here.

options.text: EntityManagerInterface shouldn't be injected into the action
options.why: That might be a style argument, but the real problem in this code is bypassing the rules.

options.text: Using the ProductId value object was a mistake
options.why: Using ProductId is actually good; it keeps the aggregate light.

questions.q: Why does the Order aggregate hold only a ProductId instead of the whole Product object?
questions.hint: How many aggregates should change in one transaction?

options.text: Product is a separate aggregate; holding the id keeps the boundary clear and only one aggregate changes per transaction
options.why: Holding the whole object tangles two aggregates together, so transactions grow and locks multiply.

options.text: A ProductId is small and saves memory, which is the only reason
options.why: Memory is a minor reason. The main one is a clean boundary and clean rules.

options.text: Doctrine can't hold more than one entity
options.why: Doctrine can; this is a design decision, not a framework limitation.

options.text: When a Product's price changes the order's price changes too, so only the id is kept
options.why: Quite the opposite: the order keeps the price from when it was created, stored in the Order itself.

questions.q: After checkout you must notify Inventory, email, Loyalty and Analytics. Every new addition means editing the checkout file, and when Loyalty is slow the order is slow too. Which design is best?
questions.hint: Think about the difference between making an announcement and calling everyone.

options.text: Checkout only announces an OrderPlaced event; the others listen on their own and work asynchronously
options.why: The announcer is loosely coupled, adding a listener doesn't mean changing checkout, and a slow listener doesn't hold up the order.

options.text: Add more timeouts to checkout and keep calling everyone as before
options.why: Timeouts limit the damage of slowness, but you still have to touch checkout to add anything new.

options.text: Cram all the services into one class inside checkout
options.why: That tangles things further, and one class would know everything.

options.text: Have every service poll checkout's database every second
options.why: It loads the database and breaks the boundary; an event is the right way.

questions.q: Which of these are good names for events?
questions.hint: An event is a fact about the past, not an instruction.

options.text: OrderPlaced
options.why: Past tense, a fact that has already happened.

options.text: PaymentReceived
options.why: Written in the past tense, and it doesn't say who should listen.

options.text: SendConfirmationEmail
options.why: This is a command: it tells one specific recipient to do a job.

options.text: ReserveStock
options.why: This is a command too. The event would be StockReserved.

questions.q: What is wrong with the naming and usage in this handler?
questions.hint: What is Sales telling the other side: reporting a fact, or giving an order?

options.text: `SendReceipt` is really a command; the event bus should carry the name of something that happened, like OrderPlaced
options.why: Sales is dictating the email service's job, so the coupling is tight again. If it reports the fact, the email service decides for itself what to do.

options.text: The handler shouldn't be final readonly
