options.why: final readonly is harmless here; the problem is the naming and the concept.

options.text: Using event.bus is wrong; everything should go through command.bus
options.why: The event bus is the right place to announce facts; the mistake is that the message is a command.

options.text: Instead of dispatch(), it should call the email class directly
options.why: That takes you back to the tight coupling you started with.

questions.q: The order list page is slow because it needs 6 joins. The write side is fine. Which CQRS step is the wisest place to start?
questions.hint: Where do you get most of the benefit for the least cost?

options.text: A separate query class on the same database, plus a flat read table (order_summary) if needed
options.why: A small step at low cost that directly fixes the slow page. Eventual consistency stays limited.

options.text: Introduce event sourcing across the whole system
options.why: The problem is the speed of one list. Event sourcing is a huge, unnecessary change.

options.text: Build a separate microservice for every class
options.why: That isn't even CQRS, and it costs far more.

options.text: Do nothing and tell users to wait
options.why: The problem is measured and a simple fix exists. There is no reason to ignore it.

questions.q: In which situations does event-driven design or CQRS not pay for itself?
questions.hint: Think about whether there is anything to gain.

options.text: One developer, a simple CRUD app, a few hundred users a day
options.why: One party and little load, so the extra cost buys nothing.

options.text: Showing a balance, where you need the exact figure the moment a transaction happens
options.why: With eventual consistency the figure can be briefly wrong, which is unacceptable here.

options.text: One order event that 5 different teams each act on separately
options.why: This is exactly where event-driven shines: many parties, one event.

options.text: Read requests outnumber writes 100 to 1 and the page is slow
options.why: Here the benefit of shaping the read side separately (CQRS) is obvious.

questions.q: Kevin's handler saves an order, then dispatches OrderPlaced to RabbitMQ. A deploy kills the process between the two lines. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: The process died, so no exception can be caught. What must be saved together?

options.text: Wrap the dispatch in try/catch and log the error
options.why: A killed process throws nothing to catch. The dispatch line simply never runs.

options.text: Dispatch the event before saving the order
options.why: Now a crash can announce an order that was never saved, and listeners act on something that does not exist.

options.text: Save the event in an outbox table in the same transaction as the order, and let a relay send it to RabbitMQ
options.why: Order and event commit together or not at all. The relay delivers the stored event, and retries until it succeeds.

options.text: Retry the whole web request after 3 seconds
options.why: The order is already saved, so a retry creates a duplicate order and still gives no guarantee about the event.

questions.q: You have 10 minutes to explain to a new product manager what our system is and who it talks to. Which picture is best?
questions.hint: They don't know the technology.

options.text: The C4 Context diagram
options.why: It shows the system, its users and the outside systems, without any internal technology.

options.text: The C4 Code diagram (a class diagram)
options.why: That is the innermost level, far too fine-grained for a new PM.

options.text: A Component diagram
options.why: It shows the parts inside a container, which is much more than the PM needs.

options.text: The full database schema
options.why: A schema is internal detail; it doesn't show the system's outside relationships.

questions.q: What happens at checkout when the Payment API times out? Which picture is best for answering that question?
questions.hint: What is the question about: structure, or order?

options.text: A sequence diagram with the happy and the timeout branch
options.why: The question is about time order and a failure branch, which a sequence diagram shows directly.

options.text: The C4 Container diagram
options.why: It shows who calls whom, but not the order or what happens on a timeout.

options.text: The C4 Context diagram
options.why: That is a higher level; it has no failure sequence.

options.text: The team's org chart
options.why: That is team structure, not the order of events in the system.

questions.q: Which of these belong in a good ADR?
questions.hint: The reason, the alternatives and the price: you need all three.

options.text: Context: what problem and what constraints, with numbers
options.why: Without the context, a future reader can't tell why the decision was made.

options.text: The alternatives that were rejected, and why
options.why: When the same proposal comes up again, the answer is here.

options.text: Consequences: both good and bad, and the trigger for revisiting
options.why: No decision is free; when the price is written down, later discussion can be honest.

options.text: The whole code, so the decision can be reproduced exactly
options.why: An ADR records the reason for a decision, not a copy of the code. The code is already in the repository.

questions.q: ADR-0007 says "email goes through Messenger's doctrine transport". A year later, 1200 messages a minute arrive, so you move to RabbitMQ. What should you do?
questions.hint: Don't erase history.

options.text: Write a new ADR-0021 and set ADR-0007's status to "Superseded by ADR-0021"
options.why: The history stays: why it was the doctrine transport before, and why it is RabbitMQ now.

options.text: Erase the text of ADR-0007 and write RabbitMQ instead
options.why: The old context and reasons are lost; in the future nobody will know why it changed.

options.text: Do nothing; the code is the truth
options.why: Code says what is there, not why, and ADR-0007 would now give wrong information.

options.text: Delete ADR-0007
options.why: Delete the history and you delete the answer to "why did we change?".

questions.q: An architecture diagram drawn in Confluence two years ago shows a service that no longer exists in the code. What is the root problem, and what is the remedy?
questions.hint: The picture is far from the code, so who will update it?

options.text: The picture is far from the code so it was never updated; make it diagram-as-code in the repository and change it in PRs
options.why: When a picture change arrives in the same review as the code change, it goes stale less.

options.text: Confluence is slow; pick a different wiki tool
options.why: Whichever wiki you use, if it is away from the code it will go stale the same way.

options.text: Drawing pictures is the mistake; reading the code is enough
options.why: Code doesn't show structure, relationships or the reasons for decisions quickly. Pictures are needed; they just need to stay fresh.

options.text: Redraw every picture from scratch once a year
options.why: With one update a year, the picture lies for the other eleven months.
